newsitem.title: Italy: FOCUS-Strike call at struggling Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strike call at struggling Olivetti.

text.p: Italian unions representing workers at Olivetti on Wednesday called a strike to protest against radical restructuring plans at the troubled information and technology group.
Earlier, the Italian stock market regulatory body Consob said it was not worried by Olivetti's financial situation but would keep a close eye on developments.

Olivetti, which has seen virtually all its top management quit in recent weeks, announced in September it would not return to profit this year as previously promised and revealed an unexpected surge in net debt.

Faced by mounting losses, new chief executive Roberto Colaninno said last week the company would sell its personal computer business, which was previously viewed as a core concern, by the end of the year.

Equity analysts have welcomed the news with relief, but Italy's three largest metal industry unions announced an eight hour strike across the Olivetti group for October 18 to protest against the plan.
"Olivetti's scientific, professional and human assets cannot be dispersed. They are assets which belong to the whole country and must be protected," a joint union statement said.
It called on Olivetti management to establish a network of national and international alliances to bring stability to the group and urged the government to prevent the PC sell-off.

Olivetti published its first half 1996 results in early September but the next day its director general in charge of finance and auditing Renzo Francesconi resigned after casting doubts on the accuracy of the figures.
Following Consob demands for further information, Olivetti announced late last month that its net group debt had nearly doubled in the two months since June to 2.4 trillion lire ($1.58 billion).
Consob produced an 18 page document on Wednesday chronicalling the Olivetti saga.

"It is not the financial position (at Olivetti) which worries us, but we want the situation to be clear and that they say how things are going," Consob chief Enzo Berlanda said before presenting the report to a parliamentary committee.

"Just as they presented data for the end of August, we will see to it that there are intermediary reports between here and the end of the year because this is a delicate phase," he said, adding that the surge in debt "had amazed us the most".
Berlanda also said that Consob was investigating whether foreign investors had recently taken large stakes in the battered group without informing the necessary authorities.

Olivetti shares were down seven lire to 520 lire by 1300 GMT having hit an early high of 545 lire following Italian press reports of possible interest in the group's PC business from Japanese giants NEC and Sony.
An NEC spokesman later said it had no such interest, while Sony rejected the rumours as "groundless".
Colaninno told financial analysts in Milan last week he planned to raise some 800 billion lire from asset sales this year and a further 400 billion lire in 1997. $1 = 1,521 lire
